questions.q: In this course, what does “14-3-3” refer to?
options: The protein that bends DNA into a loop so that a distant enhancer can reach its own promoter.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
A family of scaffold proteins, each carrying a pocket that recognises phosphate groups, which hold phosphorylated YAP in the cytoplasm and let it be degraded.
The scaffold protein that passes the MST signal on to LATS in the Hippo pathway.
questions.why: 14-3-3 is a family of scaffold proteins, each with a pocket that recognises phosphate groups. When the Hippo pathway is on, LATS1 phosphorylates YAP; the phosphorylated YAP is then seized by 14-3-3 and the whole complex is degraded, so YAP never reaches the nucleus. The other distractors are the DNA-bending protein, APOLO and SAV.

questions.q: In this course, what does “3 prime untranslated region (3 prime UTR)” refer to?
options: The stretch of mRNA between the stop codon and the poly-A tail; it is not itself translated into protein, but it concentrates miRNA seed sequences and RNA-binding protein sites.
The chemical cap on the 5′ end of the mRNA that protects the message and is recognised by the ribosomal initiation factors.
A string of adenosines added to the end of the mRNA; the longer the tail, the more translation there is.
The stretch of pre-mRNA that is cut out during splicing and does not appear in the mature mRNA.
questions.why: The 3′ UTR is the stretch of mRNA between the stop codon and the poly-A tail. It is not itself translated into protein, yet it is the most densely regulated part of the message: miRNA seed sequences, RNA-binding protein sites and the structures that determine mRNA lifetime are all concentrated here. The other distractors are the 5′ cap, the poly-A tail and the intron.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Activator” refer to?
options: The protein that sits on the operator and blocks the downstream gene.
The form of a repressor that sits on the operator but, having no ligand bound, cannot grip the DNA.
The helper protein that teams up with a repressor to press transcription down even harder.
The protein that binds the enhancer and then, by bending the DNA, pulls the transcription machinery towards the promoter.
questions.why: An activator is the helper that switches a gene on: it binds the enhancer first, then, through proteins that fold the DNA, loops the enhancer back onto a promoter thousands of bases away, recruiting RNA polymerase and the general transcription factors. The other distractors are the repressor, the apo-repressor and the co-repressor.

questions.q: A nuclear receptor has two activation domains that recruit co-activators, one at the NTD end and one at the LBD end — what are they called?
questions.why: AF-1 and AF-2 are the activation domains of a nuclear receptor that recruit co-activators: ligand binding changes the conformation of the LBD, which amounts to replacing AF-2 with a fresh binding surface, and the co-activator is then invited in. The other distractors are the core region of the promoter (core promoter), the sequence on the promoter (TATA box) and the structural motif of the DBD (zinc finger).

questions.q: In this course, what does “AGO” refer to?
options: The enzyme that cuts the primary microRNA transcript into short hairpins.
The splicing machine made of five snRNPs.
The scaffold protein of the silencing complex RISC, which carries the microRNA and uses its seed sequence to find the target mRNA.
The partner receptor that pairs with the type II nuclear receptor to form a heterodimer.
questions.why: AGO (Argonaute) is the scaffold of RISC. Once the microRNA has been cut out of its longer precursor, it is loaded into AGO, and this guide strand recognises the mRNA through the seed sequence at its 3′ end. The division of labour is clear: Drosha handles the shape, Dicer handles the length, AGO does the guiding. The other distractors are Drosha, the spliceosome and RXR.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Allolactose” refer to?
options: An isomer of lactose; it is the molecule that actually binds the Lac repressor and makes it let go of the operator.
A synthetic inducer that switches the repressor off without being metabolised by the bacteria.
The milk sugar that E. coli can use as an energy source.
The end product of the trp operon, which binds the Trp repressor and shuts the whole operon down.
questions.why: A common misconception is that “lactose present” opens the lac operon. In truth the β-galactosidase encoded by lacZ not only breaks down lactose, it also converts some of it into allolactose, and it is allolactose that actually binds the Lac repressor and makes it release the operator. IPTG is the synthetic inducer, lactose is the substrate, and tryptophan is the corepressor of trp.

questions.q: A eukaryotic mRNA can receive its poly-A tail at different polyadenylation sites, which changes the length of the 3′ UTR — what is this phenomenon called?
questions.why: Choosing the proximal PAS gives a short 3′ UTR; choosing the distal one gives a long 3′ UTR, and the longer 3′ UTR carries extra sites for RBPs, miRNAs and lncRNAs, so mRNA stability, translation efficiency and intracellular localisation all change with it. Alternative splicing changes the combination of exons, not the position of the poly-A tail.

questions.q: The same gene uses different combinations of exons to make several slightly different versions of a protein — what is this mechanism called?
questions.why: In the transcribed pre-mRNA the introns are cut out by the spliceosome and the exons joined, but splicing is not limited to one combination, so one gene can make several isoforms: MCL1 is cut into a pro-apoptotic and an anti-apoptotic version, while splicing AR's cryptic exon in produces AR-V7, which makes prostate cancer resistant to enzalutamide.

questions.q: A synNotch CAR only fires when it sees two conditions at once — what is this logic gate, in which the output is true only when both inputs are true, called?
questions.why: In logic gates the AND-gate outputs “true” only when both inputs are “true”. The synNotch design chains two signals together: synNotch first recognises tumour antigen A, and only the intracellular fragment released by cleavage then drives expression of the CAR, and the CAR itself must simultaneously recognise antigen B before it fires.

questions.q: A repressor has two forms: one whose conformation changes when a ligand binds, which can sit on the operator and block transcription; the free form that cannot grip DNA without a ligand and therefore stays loose is called ______.
questions.why: A repressor has two forms, and the contrast is clearest in the trp operon. Without tryptophan the repressor has no ligand and the wrong conformation, cannot bind the operator and has to stay loose off the DNA; this free form is the apo-repressor. The form with tryptophan bound is the active repressor.

questions.q: Of the four lncRNA prototypes, which one pairs with DNA through its own sequence and forms an RNA–DNA hybrid to take part in gene regulation?
questions.why: The lecturer's lecture five slides sort the functions of lncRNA into four prototypes: APOLO forms an RNA–DNA hybrid, PNCTR uses a YYUCUY motif to bind PTBP1 and control splicing, XIST binds SPEN and PRC2 to make epigenetic silencing, and TINCR pairs with mRNA to affect its stability. APOLO does no work itself; it delivers the machinery to the right address.

questions.q: The AR gene is aberrantly spliced so that a cryptic exon is included, producing an isoform that lacks the ligand-binding domain, is constitutively active and resists enzalutamide — what is this isoform called?
questions.why: Normal AR skips that cryptic exon CE3, whereas AR-V7 splices it in; the resulting protein lacks the ligand-binding domain and so is already active without any ligand, which makes prostate cancer resistant to enzalutamide and the patient relapse.

questions.q: When the repressor is still sitting on the operator and RNA polymerase can only just squeeze past, the small amount of mRNA produced is called what?
questions.why: Transcription comes in two strengths. While the repressor is still on the operator, RNA polymerase can only just get past and very little mRNA is made; that is basal transcription, also called low-level expression. For his teaching of the lac operon this is the key fourth state — when lactose is present but glucose is plentiful, the gene is on but slow.

questions.q: In this course, what does “calcium ions” refer to?
options: An intracellular second messenger: IP₃ triggers release of calcium ions from the endoplasmic reticulum, and the rise in concentration is itself the signal.
A small second messenger whose concentration rises when glucose is low, allowing CAP to bring RNA polymerase to the promoter.
The chemical cap at the front of the mRNA, which protects the message and calls the ribosome to collect it.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
questions.why: IP₃ travels from the cell membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum, binds IP₃ receptors in the ER membrane and releases the stored calcium ions into the cytoplasm; the rise in calcium concentration is itself a signal that activates downstream proteins such as calmodulin. Calcium signalling is fast because the cytoplasmic calcium concentration is normally very low, so any release immediately creates a clear gradient. The other distractors are cAMP, the 5′ cap and APOLO.

questions.q: In this course, what does “cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate)” refer to?
options: The enzyme that cuts long RNA short; one of its products becomes a microRNA.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
The protein that bends DNA into a loop so that a distant enhancer can reach its own promoter.
A small second messenger whose concentration rises when glucose is low and which, once bound to CAP, sits on the promoter and drives transcription up.
questions.why: cAMP is cyclic AMP, a small molecule that can diffuse everywhere — a classic second messenger. In the bacterial lac operon it acts as the reporter of energy status: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and binds CAP, the complex forms and sits on the promoter to pull RNA polymerase in, and transcription goes from slow to strong.

questions.q: In this course, what does “CAP” refer to?
options: A second messenger that carries signals from outside the cell deep into the cytoplasm.
The bacterial positive regulator, which has no activity of its own and must bind cAMP before it can sit on the promoter.
A reporter gene that puts a promoter fragment in front of it in order to measure how active transcription is.
The helper protein that teams up with a repressor to press transcription down even harder.
questions.why: CAP is catabolite activator protein, a positive regulator in E. coli. It has no activity of its own and only works once it has bound cAMP to become the cAMP–CAP complex; this complex sits directly on the promoter to recruit RNA polymerase, so transcription of the lac genes goes from slow to strong.

questions.q: The 5′ end of a eukaryotic mRNA carries a 7-methylguanine cap that protects the message, helps with export and is recognised by the ribosomal initiation factors — this cap is called ______.
questions.why: The 5′ cap has three functions: it protects the mRNA from being chewed up from the 5′ end by nucleases, it helps the mRNA be exported from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and it is recognised by the ribosomal initiation factors to start translation. mRNA without a cap is far less efficient, which is a key design point in mRNA vaccines.

questions.q: When glucose is low, cAMP rises and binds CAP, and the resulting complex sits directly on the promoter and pulls transcription from slow to strong — this complex is called ______.
questions.why: This is the accelerator of the lac operon. But note its powers: CAP can only be added to a system that the repressor has already released. In the four states on his lecture five slides, the last one is that the cAMP–CAP complex is present but the repressor is still sitting on the operator, and the result is still blocked.

questions.q: Neurons and hepatocytes carry the same DNA yet express completely different lists of genes; the same gene is switched on in some cell types and off in others — what is this phenomenon called?
questions.why: Every cell in a person carries the same DNA, but the difference comes from the different combinations of transcription factors present in each cell type, so the same promoter is watched by different activators and repressors in different cells. He ties this to time specificity and marks it as always emphasize.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Central dogma” refer to?
options: The mechanism by which one gene uses different exon combinations to make several versions of a protein.
The rule that genetic information flows one way: a DNA sequence serves as a template for RNA, and an RNA sequence serves as a template for protein.
The small proteins that pass messages over short distances between cells.
The whole process of switching a gene on, copying out the message and then making the protein.
questions.why: The central dogma says that a DNA sequence can serve as a template for making RNA and an RNA sequence can serve as a template for making protein. The full sequence in class is: DNA is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus, the mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm, the ribosome follows it to join amino acids into a polypeptide, and that folds into a protein.

questions.q: What is the collective name for regulatory sequences such as promoter, enhancer, silencer and insulator that act only on the DNA molecule they sit on?
questions.why: “Cis” means “on the same side”: these regulatory sequences can act only on the gene on the DNA molecule next to them, even when the cell holds two copies of the same gene. The cis elements and the diffusible trans factors that can act across chromosomes are the contrast he lists among his distractors.

questions.q: When ligand binding changes the conformation of the LBD of a nuclear receptor and AF-2 becomes a fresh binding surface, what is the protein that is invited in to help drive transcription called?
questions.why: When ligand binding changes the conformation of the LBD, the AF-2 region becomes a new docking surface that pulls in the co-activator; these co-activators carry enzymatic activity themselves, acetylating histones, loosening the chromatin and bringing RNA polymerase in. What docks in the absence of ligand is the co-repressor.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Co-repressor (nuclear receptor)” refer to?
options: The protein that the nuclear receptor invites in after ligand binding, which acetylates histones and drives transcription.
The protein itself that sits on the operator and blocks transcription.
The molecule that binds the ligand-binding domain of the nuclear receptor and changes its conformation.
The protein that is docked by the LBD of the nuclear receptor when there is no ligand, recruiting HDAC to compact the chromatin.
questions.why: The nuclear receptor is a two-way switch. Without ligand, the LBD of the receptor docks a co-repressor, which recruits deacetylating enzymes such as HDAC to compact the chromatin and keep the gene off; when ligand arrives this is swapped for a co-activator, the enzymes become acetyltransferases, the chromatin loosens. What decides the switch is not whether the receptor is present but which set of proteins is docked on it.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Core promoter” refer to?
options: A sequence thousands of bases from the gene that raises transcription by bending the DNA.
A short stretch of DNA immediately upstream of the transcription start site (+1), where the transcription initiation complex is assembled, usually with a TATA box around −30.
A sequence that turns transcription down and can sit upstream or downstream of the gene.
A DNA sequence that stops an enhancer acting on the wrong gene.
questions.why: Eukaryotic gene activation has two layers. The core promoter is a short stretch immediately upstream of the transcription start site (+1), usually with a TATAAA box around −30; the transcription initiation complex is assembled there: TFIID (containing TBP) recognises the TATA first, and the other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II then join one by one. The other distractors are the enhancer, the silencer and the insulator.

questions.q: A repressor generally needs a partner before it can really press transcription down — what is that partner called? In the trp operon it is tryptophan.
questions.why: When tryptophan is plentiful in the cell it binds the Trp repressor as a corepressor, so the complex changes conformation, can sit on the operator, and the genes for making tryptophan are switched off — negative feedback, and the mirror image of the logic of the trp and lac operons.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Cryptic exon” refer to?
options: A stretch of sequence that is not treated as an exon at all until a mutation creates new splice sites and switches it on.
The stretch that is skipped during splicing and never enters the mature mRNA.
A new splice site created in an intron by a single base substitution.
A slightly different version of a protein produced by a gene that uses different combinations of exons.
questions.why: Some sequences are never treated as exons under normal conditions and are only switched on when a mutation creates new splice sites; that is a cryptic exon. His lecture five slides illustrate this with AR: normal AR skips the cryptic exon CE3, whereas AR-V7 splices it in, producing an isoform that lacks the ligand-binding domain and is resistant to enzalutamide.

questions.q: In this course, what does “CTGF” refer to?
options: Vascular endothelial growth factor, switched on by HIF-1α so that the tumour builds its own vessels.
The hypoxia-inducible factor, which is marked for destruction once the hydroxylase enzymes have added a hydroxyl group to it.
A long non-coding RNA that silences an entire X chromosome.
Connective tissue growth factor; one of the target genes switched on by YAP through TEAD when Hippo is off, promoting fibroblast proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition.
questions.why: When the Hippo pathway is off, unphosphorylated YAP enters the nucleus, binds TEAD and switches on a set of growth-promoting genes; his slides list CTGF, JAG1 and NOTCH2. CTGF promotes fibroblast proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition and lies at the core of tissue fibrosis and the tumour stromal reaction. The other distractors are VEGF, HIF-1α and XIST.

questions.q: The small proteins that carry messages over short distances between cells, secreted to act on nearby cells, are called ______; TNF-α and IL-1β, secreted after NF-κB is activated, belong to this family.
questions.why: Cytokines are the short-range messages between cells, secreted to act on nearby cells. His lecture five uses NF-κB to show the time course of these signals: TNF-α peaks at 4–6 hours, then IL-1β, then IFN-γ, and finally IL-2 and IL-15. The ordering reflects upstream and downstream causality, and the cytokines that are secreted feed back to strengthen NF-κB activation.

questions.q: Everything inside the cell membrane but outside the nucleus is called ______; glycolysis, protein synthesis and most metabolic reactions take place there.
questions.why: The cytoplasm is everything inside the cell membrane and outside the nucleus, made up roughly of water plus dissolved ions, small molecules, proteins and many suspended organelles. Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so the whole cytoplasm is their workspace and transcription and translation can happen at the same time.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Delta ligand” refer to?
options: The molecule on the surface of a neighbouring cell, which only starts signalling when it touches Notch on the receiving cell.
The receptor on the cell surface used to detect delta on the surface of neighbouring cells.
The fragment cut out of the membrane by a protease, released and carried into the nucleus.
An artificial Notch receptor used to recognise tumour antigens.
questions.why: Notch is a “neighbour sensor”. The Notch receptor on the receiving cell carries EGF repeats and is responsible for making contact with the delta ligand on the other cell's surface; after contact Notch is cleaved by a protease, releasing the intracellular NICD, which moves into the nucleus to switch on genes. The key point is that delta is present only on neighbouring cells, so the Notch system comes with positional information built in.

questions.q: The same gene has a different on/off timetable in the embryonic, childhood and adult periods — what is this phenomenon called?
questions.why: Gene expression changes not only with cell type but also with time, with the embryonic, childhood and adult periods each having their own timetable for switching genes on and off. He places this alongside cell-type specificity and says both are concepts to always emphasize.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Dicer” refer to?
options: The enzyme that cuts the primary miRNA transcript into short hairpins inside the nucleus.
The enzyme that cuts pre-miRNA into a double strand of about 22 nucleotides, and the source of siRNA.
The protein that partners with Drosha so that Drosha can recognise the hairpin it should cut.
The silencing complex protein that carries the microRNA and guides recognition of the target mRNA.
questions.why: miRNA production has two steps: upstream, the Microprocessor (DGCR8 plus Drosha) cuts pri-miRNA into pre-miRNA in the nucleus, pre-miRNA is exported to the cytoplasm by Exportin-5, and DICER1 plus TRBP then cuts it into a double strand of about 22 nucleotides. The division of labour is Drosha for the shape, Dicer for the length and AGO for the guiding.

questions.q: Nuclear receptor monomers bind DNA response elements very poorly and need to work in pairs to read the DNA accurately — this phenomenon is called ______.
questions.why: Nuclear receptor monomers bind DNA response elements very poorly and need two together to read the DNA accurately, which is why the DBD of a nuclear receptor has zinc finger structures and almost always acts as a dimer. Symmetrical homodimers and asymmetrical heterodimers both work.

questions.q: In this course, what does “DNA-bending protein” refer to?
options: The protein that grips the DNA between the enhancer and the promoter and bends them into a loop.
A family of scaffold proteins, each carrying a pocket that recognises phosphate groups.
The enzyme that cuts long RNA short, one of whose products becomes a microRNA.
The enzyme that copies the base sequence of DNA into RNA.
questions.why: An enhancer can sit thousands of bases away from the gene and still control how much that gene is transcribed, because DNA is itself flexible: a class of proteins called DNA-bending proteins grips the DNA between the enhancer and the promoter and bends them into a loop, letting the activator bound at the enhancer touch the machinery at the promoter.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Drosha” refer to?
options: The enzyme that cuts pre-miRNA into a double strand of about 22 nucleotides.
The scaffold protein of the silencing complex RISC, which carries the microRNA.
The transport receptor that carries short hairpin RNA out of the nucleus.
The enzyme that forms the Microprocessor with DGCR8 and cuts pri-miRNA into a roughly 70-nucleotide hairpin in the nucleus.
questions.why: Drosha and its partner protein DGCR8 form the Microprocessor, which cuts the primary transcript (pri-miRNA) into a hairpin of about 70 nucleotides (pre-miRNA); Exportin-5 then carries it out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm, and Dicer cuts it into a double strand of about 22 nucleotides. Drosha is therefore the gatekeeper that decides which stretch of RNA is eligible to become a regulatory signal.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Endometrium” refer to?
options: Breast tissue; there tamoxifen blocks estrogen and inhibits proliferation.
The endometrium; there tamoxifen is a partial agonist, whereas in breast tissue it is an antagonist.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
The region of a nuclear receptor that binds the ligand and changes conformation on binding.
questions.why: In the breast tamoxifen is an antagonist: estrogen is kept out of the receptor, co-activators cannot be recruited and the cells stop proliferating; in the endometrium it is a partial agonist and can recruit co-activators to promote proliferation, so the risk of endometrial cancer rises slightly.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Enhanceosome” refer to?
options: The complex of five snRNPs that splices in the nucleus.
The full set of general transcription factors that forms the pre-initiation complex together with RNA polymerase II.
A complex of transcription factors and co-activators acting together, which recruits RNA polymerase II at the enhancer and the promoter.
The molecular chaperone that holds a folded receptor in the cytoplasm.
questions.why: The enhanceosome is a complex formed by a group of transcription factors and co-activators acting together. His lecture five slides draw it as bound to enhancer + promoter → gene to be controlled: an activator occupies the enhancer first and DNA-bending proteins pull it into a loop. A single activator is usually not enough to drive transcription.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Enhancer” refer to?
options: A DNA sequence that raises transcription, which can sit thousands of bases upstream of the gene or on the downstream 3′ side of the gene.
A DNA sequence that turns transcription down, which can sit upstream, downstream or even inside an intron.
A DNA sequence that stops an enhancer acting on the wrong gene, marking the boundaries of a gene.
The DNA word that tells RNA polymerase where to start transcribing, with a TATA box around −30.
questions.why: An enhancer is a stretch of DNA that raises transcription, and its position is relatively independent: it can sit thousands of bases upstream of the gene, or downstream of it, on the 3′ side. He particularly stresses a common misconception: not all enhancers are upstream.

questions.q: In this course, what does “EPO” refer to?
options: Vascular endothelial growth factor, which makes nearby vascular endothelium grow new vessels into the tumour.
The glucose transporter switched on by HIF-1α, which lets cells keep working without oxygen.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
Erythropoietin; the haematopoietic growth factor switched on by HIF-1α that acts on red cell precursors in the bone marrow.
questions.why: EPO is the haematopoietic growth factor, produced mainly by the kidney. When hypoxia stabilises HIF-1α, which enters the nucleus and binds HIF-1β, the HRE opens up EPO and a whole set of genes alongside it; EPO rises, red cell production increases and the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity is restored. The other distractors are VEGF, GLUT1 and APOLO.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Estrogen receptor (ER)” refer to?
options: The DNA word that the estrogen receptor binds in dimer form.
The nuclear receptor for estrogen; without estrogen it is held in the cytoplasm by HSP90, and only after ligand binding does it dimerise, enter the nucleus, recruit co-activators and bind ERE.
A drug that competes with estrogen for the same binding site but blocks the receptor in breast tissue while activating it in the endometrium.
The protein that is tagged with ubiquitin after binding estrogen and sent to the proteasome for degradation.
questions.why: ER is a type I nuclear receptor. Without ligand it is held in the cytoplasm by a chaperone such as HSP90; once estrogen binds, HSP90 lets go, the receptor dimerises, enters the nucleus, recruits co-activators and finally binds ERE to switch on genes. The key to the whole mechanism is the change in receptor conformation. The other distractors are ERE, tamoxifen, and the one about being tagged with ubiquitin after binding estrogen and sent to the proteasome.

questions.q: The specific DNA sequence that the estrogen receptor binds in dimer form — the “word” the receptor recognises on DNA — is called ______.
questions.why: The DBD of ER recognises this word as a dimer, and recognises only this one, so different response elements determine which genes a receptor acts on. For drug development the ERE sequence can be used in a reporter assay: attach a candidate promoter fragment in front of luciferase, delete it piece by piece and measure the activity of the reporter gene.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Exon” refer to?
options: The part of a gene that is retained after splicing and enters the mature mRNA.
The part of a gene that is cut out during splicing and does not appear in the mature mRNA.
A stretch of sequence that is not treated as an exon at all until a mutation creates new splice sites and switches it on.
A slightly different version of a protein produced by a gene that uses different combinations of exons.
questions.why: Although an exon is called an expressed region, it is really the part that is shown, whereas an intron is the part that is hidden — the names are the other way round, a classic point of confusion in this course. The mouse β-globin slide makes it clear: Exon 1, Intron 1, Exon 2, Intron 2, Exon 3, and only after splicing does it become a mature mRNA with a 5′ UTR, three exons and a 3′ UTR.

questions.q: The spliceosome makes competing choices near splice sites, deciding whether a given exon is kept; what is the collective name for the two opposite moves of including an exon in the mature mRNA and skipping it entirely?
questions.why: One gene can therefore produce several isoforms, for example the pro-apoptotic MCL-1S and anti-apoptotic MCL-1L, and Bcl-x(L) and Bcl-x(S). Exon skipping can also be pathological: in his liver cancer case a single-nucleotide variant inside an intron created a new splice site, so exon 7 was skipped altogether and overall survival was clearly worse (P < 0.001).

questions.q: In this course, what does “Exportin-5” refer to?
options: The enzyme that forms the Microprocessor with DGCR8 and cuts pre-miRNA out in the nucleus.
The nuclear export receptor that works with Ran-GTP to carry the pre-miRNA hairpin from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
The enzyme that cuts pre-miRNA into a double strand of about 22 nucleotides.
The partner receptor that pairs with the type II nuclear receptor to form a heterodimer.
questions.why: Exportin-5 (XPO5, the nuclear export receptor) works with Ran-GTP to carry the pre-miRNA hairpin cut out by Drosha from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. The principle is a directional cargo label: only when Ran-GTP is bound to XPO5 does it seize RNA carrying a nuclear export signal.

questions.q: The whole process of switching a gene on, copying out the message and then making the protein, made up of the two arrows from DNA to RNA (transcription) and from RNA to protein (translation), is called what?
questions.why: Gene expression is a pipeline made of three arrows, and every arrow is a stage that can be regulated, hence also a stage that can be drugged. Most clinical biomarkers work through regulation of gene expression, and the same mutation (BRCA, for instance) does not guarantee disease precisely because the regulatory layer decides it.

questions.q: The same DNA read out into a different combination of genes in different cell types — that combination is the cell's identity. What is it called?
questions.why: The difference comes from each cell type expressing different transcription factors, and different transcription factors switch on different enhancers, so which genes are on is decided by cellular identity. His t-SNE clustering plot separates PBMC and melanoma and ascites samples into macrophage, cancer cell, T cell, NK cell, dendritic cell, CAF, endothelial cell, B cell and so on precisely by their expression profiles.

questions.q: In this course, what does “General transcription factor” refer to?
options: A protein that works for one particular gene only, binding the enhancer and helping to recruit the polymerase.
The protein that binds the operator and blocks the downstream gene.
The protein that binds the TATA box on the promoter and bends the DNA by about 90 degrees.
The general transcription factors needed to start transcription at any gene, unrelated to which gene it is, whose only job is to assemble the machinery.
questions.why: The general transcription factors are these basic parts that have nothing to do with which gene it is and whose only job is to assemble the machinery: TFIID (containing TBP), TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH. What really decides which gene is switched on is the sequence-specific transcription factors and the enhancers.

questions.q: The genetic make-up of a cell or a person — the version of each gene it carries — is called what?
questions.why: Genotype is the genetic composition (which version you carry), while phenotype is the appearance that is expressed. A whole regulatory chain lies between the two, so genotype does not equal phenotype: the same BRCA mutation makes one person ill and another not.

questions.q: In this course, what does “GLUT1” refer to?
options: The haematopoietic growth factor produced mainly by the kidney that acts on red cell precursors in the bone marrow.
The growth factor that makes nearby vascular endothelium grow new vessels into the tumour.
The membrane transporter that brings glucose into the cell, switched on by HIF-1α through an HRE when there is hypoxia.
The protein that recognises hydroxylated HIF-1α under normal oxygen and hands it to the proteasome.
questions.why: Under hypoxia HIF-1α is stabilised, enters the nucleus and binds HIF-1β, and the HRE opens up VEGF, GLUT1 and EPO as a group. Opening GLUT1 means that even without oxygen the cell can bring in more glucose and keep going on glycolysis.

questions.q: The processing step that attaches sugar trees to proteins, usually completed in the rough ER and partly modified further in the Golgi, is called ______.
questions.why: The sugar groups are like labels: they protect the protein from breakdown, help it fold and decide where it finally ends up. The clinical consequence is direct: cells and bacteria glycosylate proteins differently, so bacterial proteins are often attacked by the human immune system as foreign — this is why mammalian cells (CHO cells) are used to make therapeutic proteins.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Guide (lncRNA)” refer to?
options: Long non-coding RNA that binds two or more proteins together in the right place.
Long non-coding RNA that pairs with DNA through its own sequence and forms an RNA–DNA hybrid.
Long non-coding RNA that binds SPEN and PRC2 to silence an entire X chromosome.
Long non-coding RNA that uses one stretch of sequence to recognise a specific position in the genome and then brings chromatin-modifying enzymes or transcription factors there.
questions.why: This is one of the two ways lncRNA work. The guide itself has no catalytic ability, but it uses one stretch of sequence to recognise a specific place in the genome and then delivers chromatin-modifying enzymes or transcription factors there to do their work. The other distractors are the scaffold, APOLO and XIST.

questions.q: The HER receptor family has four members, three of which are HER1 (that is, EGFR), HER3 and HER4; what is the structural fact about them together with HER2?
options: All three are nuclear receptors that bind estrogen.
They form heterodimers with HER2 to switch on downstream signalling, whereas HER2 homodimerises very inefficiently on its own.
All three are held in the cytoplasm by HSP90 while they wait for a ligand.
Their DNA-binding domains are made entirely of zinc fingers.
questions.why: The key structural fact is that HER2 pairs with itself very inefficiently; it mostly forms heterodimers with HER1, HER3 or HER4, and dimerisation is what switches on downstream signalling. Trastuzumab works precisely because it blocks the dimerisation of HER2 with HER3.

questions.q: Before using a HER2 drug you have to confirm the patient is HER2 positive; what is the interpretation threshold when counting by FISH?
options: HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 0.2, or HER2 copy number ≥ 6
HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0, or HER2 copy number ≥ 16
HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0, or HER2 copy number ≥ 6
questions.why: Before using the drug you have to know whether the patient is HER2 positive, so a companion diagnostic is needed: IHC or FISH, and the interpretation threshold is a HER2/CEP17 (the centromere probe of chromosome 17) ratio ≥ 2.0 or a copy number ≥ 6. The other distractors are two wrong interpretation thresholds (ratio ≥ 0.2, copy number ≥ 16) and receptor occupancy, which is a separate question about dosing.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Heterodimer” refer to?
options: A dimer made of two different protein subunits, for example HER2 and HER3.
A dimer made of two identical protein subunits.
An RNA message that carries several genes at once.
A molecule that binds two or more proteins together in the right place.
questions.why: A heterodimer is made of two different subunits, the opposite of a homodimer. For HER2 the heterodimer is almost its only normal way of working: it pairs with itself inefficiently and mainly signals by pairing with HER1/HER3/HER4, and trastuzumab blocks exactly this pairing.

questions.q: At normal oxygen, PHD and FIH hydroxylate HIF-1α, VHL recognises it and adds polyubiquitination, and it is sent to the proteasome for degradation; when there is hypoxia this route is interrupted and HIF-1α can enter the nucleus — this oxygen-sensing protein is called ______.
questions.why: The point of the whole mechanism is that oxygen is not detected directly but is translated into protein stability through oxygen-dependent enzyme activity. HIF-1β is the constant scaffold, and it is the HIF-1α half that is regulated by oxygen; the other distractors are the gatekeeper VHL and the co-activator p300/CBP, which is recruited to acetylate histones.

questions.q: In this course, what does “HIF-1β” refer to?
options: The gatekeeper that recognises hydroxylated HIF-1α and hands it to the proteasome.
Also called ARNT: a far more stable partner that is present even at normal oxygen levels.
The co-activator recruited after HIF-1α enters the nucleus to acetylate histones and loosen the chromatin.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
questions.why: HIF-1β provides the constant scaffold and HIF-1α provides the switch that rises and falls with oxygen; only together are they the complete factor that can bind the HRE and start transcription. This one-stable, one-moving design also explains why the same oxygen signal can have several outputs.

questions.q: Putting the expression of the CAR gene under the control of an HRE, so that the T cell only arms itself and fires in the hypoxic core of a tumour — what is this design called?
questions.why: The CAR protein is made only in cells where HIF-1 is active, and HIF-1 is active only when there is hypoxia, so this CAR-T is switched on only in the hypoxic core of the tumour and bypasses the oxygenated normal tissue around it. On returning to normal oxygen, the HIF-CAR signal falls below 0.2 within 2 to 3 hours.

questions.q: A dimer made of two identical protein subunits, the opposite of a heterodimer — what is it called?
questions.why: Homodimers are very common among receptors and transcription factors: the DBD of a nuclear receptor usually binds a response element as a dimer, and monomers bind DNA very poorly, so dimerisation greatly raises affinity — dimerisation is itself a regulatory switch.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Hormone” refer to?
options: The small proteins that carry messages over short distances between cells and act only on nearby cells.
The molecule that binds a receptor and changes the receptor's shape once bound.
The partner receptor that pairs with the type II nuclear receptor to form a heterodimer.
The chemical messenger secreted by a gland into the blood, carried around the body to act on distant cells.
questions.why: What separates a hormone from an ordinary signalling molecule is distance: local signals have a limited range, whereas a hormone can act a long way away and is effective at very low doses — which is precisely why he explains dosing in terms of receptor occupancy.

questions.q: In this course, what does “HSP90” refer to?
options: The protein that grips DNA at the TATA box on the promoter and bends the DNA by about 90 degrees.
The molecular chaperone that keeps the receptor folded in the cytoplasm until the ligand arrives.
The protein that partners with Drosha so that Drosha can recognise the hairpin it should cut.
One component of the complex that splices introns out in the nucleus.
questions.why: In type I receptors the receptor is caught by HSP90 in the absence of ligand and held in the cytoplasm in a ready-but-loaded conformation; when the ligand arrives HSP90 lets go, the receptor dimerises and enters the nucleus. Because HSP90 is also the chaperone for many oncoproteins, it is itself a popular drug target.

questions.q: The core of a tumour is chronically short of blood supply and therefore hypoxic, which stabilises HIF-1α and switches on the whole set of adaptive responses such as VEGF and GLUT1 through the HRE — this state of too little oxygen is called ______.
questions.why: The mechanism is not direct sensing of oxygen but loss of function of the oxygen-dependent hydroxylating enzymes (PHD, FIH), so HIF-1α is no longer marked for degradation. His figure is that about 50% of solid tumours contain hypoxic tissue, and HIF-CAR borrows this switch.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Hypoxia-responsive element (HRE)” refer to?
options: A specific DNA sequence that is recognised when HIF-1α and HIF-1β bind in the nucleus and is used to switch on transcription.
The DNA word bound by the estrogen receptor dimer.
The region around −30 on the promoter where the transcription machinery is assembled.
The stretch at the 3′ end of the mRNA that carries regulatory sites but is not translated.
questions.why: Every gene controlled by an HRE is on the list of things to do when oxygen is short: VEGF to bring vessels in, GLUT1 to bring glucose in, EPO to make more red cells. HRE has another use too, in engineering: put the gene you want expressed (most typically a CAR) under an HRE and you have a switch that works only when there is hypoxia.

questions.q: In the time course of the NF-κB inflammatory response, the cytokine that comes after TNF-α and before IFN-γ, that matures by having its precursor cleaved by caspase-1, and that acts on the hypothalamus to change the temperature set point is called what?
questions.why: He says explicitly not to worry about the order of these cytokines; it is only to let you see that different responses can be observed at different times; but these four cytokines form the backbone of his NF-κB section. IL-1β is also an endogenous pyrogen, so fever is actually the result of IL-1β and TNF-α acting.

questions.q: The gene for the protein is already wired up and the machinery is already assembled, but the whole pathway stays off until an inducer arrives, so no energy is wasted in making it — what is this ready-made, switched-on-demand design called?
questions.why: This matters particularly for recombinant expression: let E. coli grow enough first and then switch on expression of the target protein, which gives better efficiency and better folding quality. His example is the lac operon: without lactose the repressor sits on the operator and blocks the polymerase; with lactose, allolactose binds the repressor and makes it leave.

questions.q: In the lac system, the act of adding an inducer to switch a gene on is called ______; and the real inducer is actually lactose first converted into allolactose.
questions.why: Induction is the act of flipping the switch on. Once allolactose binds the repressor, the repressor changes conformation and can no longer grip the operator, so the gene starts to be transcribed — but that is only the first condition. The second condition is that glucose must be low, so that cAMP rises and CAP–cAMP binds the promoter and recruits the polymerase; only when both conditions hold do you get strong transcription.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Insulator” refer to?
options: A DNA sequence that binds particular proteins, limits the range of an enhancer and stops it acting on the wrong gene.
A stretch of DNA that turns transcription down and can sit upstream, downstream or even inside an intron.
A stretch of DNA that raises transcription and can sit thousands of bases upstream of the gene.
The protein that sits on the operator and blocks the polymerase.
questions.why: Because enhancers act in a relatively position-independent way while cell-type and time-specific expression demands precise control, a wall is needed. The insulator binds particular proteins and confines the range of an enhancer to the correct promoter, before or after it. The other distractors are the silencer, the enhancer, and the protein that sits on the operator and blocks the polymerase.

questions.q: The stretch of sequence in pre-mRNA that the spliceosome cuts out and discards, interleaved with the exons, is called ______; introns also hide microRNAs and other non-coding RNAs.
questions.why: Splicing is not arbitrary: mutations in the boundary sequences can cause a splice site to be used wrongly or to be created, so that exons are wrongly retained or skipped. His liver cancer case is a single-nucleotide variant inside an intron that creates a new splice site, leading to exon 7 being skipped and clearly worse overall survival in patients.

questions.q: What is the synthetic inducer used in recombinant expression to release the Lac repressor, switching the system off but not being metabolised by the bacteria, so its concentration stays stable, called?
questions.why: IPTG is isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside, a lactose analogue. It binds the Lac repressor and changes its conformation so that it leaves the operator, but bacteria have no enzyme that can break it down. The usual arrangement puts the target gene under a T7 promoter and keeps the lacO site, and his slides point to 100 µM as the point of optimal expression.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Isoform” refer to?
options: A stretch of sequence that is not treated as an exon at all until a mutation switches it on.
A new splice site created in an intron by a single base substitution.
A slightly different version of a protein produced by the same gene using different combinations of exons.
A long non-coding RNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
questions.why: The clinical significance has three layers: different isoforms may have different functions; a given isoform may lose its drug-binding site and so cause resistance (AR-V7 against enzalutamide); and aberrant splicing can create neoantigens. In addition, choosing different polyadenylation sites can also produce isoforms: the short version of BDNF stays near the cell body while the long version is transported into dendrites.

questions.q: When the cell is quiet, the p50 and p65 of NF-κB are held in the cytoplasm by an inhibitory protein; when the signal arrives IKK phosphorylates this inhibitor, it is ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome, and NF-κB can enter the nucleus. What is this inhibitory protein called?
questions.why: The complication is that the proteins NF-κB transcribes (including TNF-α and IL-1β) then go back and activate NF-κB, forming a positive feedback loop, which is why the inflammatory response arrives so fast and so violently. He states explicitly that LPS → TLR4 → IKK → IκB → NF-κB → nucleus is an exam question type he has already announced.

questions.q: The bacterial switch in which lacZ, lacY and lacA share one promoter and one operator and are transcribed together into a single polycistronic mRNA, and which requires both lactose present and glucose low for strong expression, is called what?
questions.why: With one condition missing, only a weak basal amount is left. This design makes the bacteria build large amounts of the sugar-digesting machinery only when they really are short of sugar, and the trp operon is its exact mirror image: when tryptophan is plentiful it switches off its own synthesis genes.

questions.q: The protein that, simply by sitting on the stretch of DNA called the operator, stops the polymerase transcribing the genes behind it; what really releases it is the isomer lactose turns into automatically, allolactose. This protein is called ______.
questions.why: As soon as allolactose binds the repressor its shape changes and it leaves the operator. Recombinant experiments often use the synthetic inducer IPTG, which is not metabolised and allows precise control of when expression starts. The other distractors are the switch of the trp operon, the form of the repressor without ligand, and the molecule that partners with the repressor.

questions.q: The disaccharide made of one glucose and one galactose, for which the three genes of the lac operon really exist — what is this molecule called?
questions.why: The cell is only worth opening this machinery when it really is short of sugar, so the default state of the switch is off. He also makes clear that IPTG is a synthetic, non-metabolised inducer, while the molecule that actually binds the repressor is the lactose isomer allolactose.

questions.q: When the Hippo pathway is off, unphosphorylated YAP can slip into the nucleus and bind TEAD, switching on genes such as CTGF, JAG1 and NOTCH2 so that tissue overgrows. Which kinase phosphorylates YAP and holds it in the cytoplasm?
questions.why: The Hippo signal runs: MST1 is phosphorylated and activates SAV, and SAV then activates LATS1. LATS1 is the brake of Hippo — YAP is held down by it, which amounts to blocking the signal to keep dividing outside the nucleus; when it fails, unphosphorylated YAP can enter the nucleus.

questions.q: The molecule whose shape fits the binding site of a receptor exactly, which changes the shape of the receptor on binding so that the signal can pass on, is called ______; it can be a hormone, a drug or a growth factor.
questions.why: The relationship between ligand and receptor is like a key and a lock. The class divides the thing into two positions: an extracellular ligand binds a receptor on the cell membrane, and an intracellular ligand binds a nuclear receptor in the cytoplasm. The other distractors are the receiver, the co-activator and the channel in the nuclear envelope.

questions.q: In this course, what does “LncRNA (long non-coding RNA)” refer to?
options: An lncRNA that forms an RNA–DNA hybrid with DNA.
RNA longer than 200 nucleotides that does not encode protein.
The lncRNA that uses a YYUCUY motif to bind PTBP1 and thereby control splicing.
The lncRNA that pairs with mRNA and then grabs Staufen 1, controlling the stability of the message.
questions.why: More than 200 nucleotides is the dividing line between it and the small RNAs. It works in two ways: as a scaffold it binds two or more proteins together in the right place, and as a guide it brings proteins to the DNA word where they should act. He also points out that it is an emerging drug-discovery target and biomarker.

questions.q: What is the gene that glows, and so is most commonly used as the reporter gene to measure how active a given stretch of promoter is, called?
questions.why: The logic of a reporter assay is this: attach a stretch of the candidate promoter in front of the luciferase gene, transfect it into cells, then measure the light that comes out. The light is a proxy for promoter activity; next you do serial deletion to find which stretch is really doing the work.

questions.q: What is the short RNA of about 22 nucleotides that represses translation by pairing, through the seed sequence at positions 2 to 8 of its 3′ end, with the 3′ UTR of the target mRNA called?
questions.why: Its production is a chain: RNA polymerase II makes the primary miRNA, Drosha cuts it into the hairpin of pre-miRNA, exportin-5 takes it out of the nucleus, Dicer cuts it into a double strand, and it is finally loaded onto AGO to form RISC. Because recognition rests on only 7 bases, one miRNA can repress hundreds or thousands of target mRNAs at once.

questions.q: The lifetime of a eukaryotic mRNA is decided by three features — the 5′ cap, the length of the poly-A tail, and the RNA-binding proteins and miRNAs bound on the 3′ UTR; what is the name for how long an mRNA survives before it is broken down?
questions.why: If the tail is trimmed short, or if miRNA and RISC drag it off to a P-body for degradation, the message retires early. His rule is worth keeping straight: a longer poly-A tail means more translation, not a longer life.
